What predicts lowering the income people expect to need at age 30?

A short plain-language report for the NGO. Question 7 in the SEARCH / NIRMAN series.

The answer in two sentencesThe people most likely to lower the monthly income they expect to need at age 30 are those who started with a high figure: 88% of the highest starters lowered it, against 33% of the lowest. Nothing else we measured before the workshop (life priorities, career plans, life satisfaction, gender, age) predicted it, and much of the pattern is simply very high first guesses coming back down.

1. The question the NGO asked

"What factors predict the reduction in monthly income expected for financial security at the age of 30, as measured by the question 'Expected Monthly Income At the Age 30'?"

Measured on Point-1 workshops (Workshop_Level 0.1), comparing each person's Pre and Post answer to Financial_Expected_Income_Age_30. "Reduction" means the Post figure is lower than the Pre figure.

Why it matters to NIRMAN: the project schema lists "lower income expectation" as one of the secondary signs of a participant's transformation towards the social sector, next to switching to full-time social action (Q1).

63%lowered the income they expect to need at 30
₹50,000typical drop per month
33% → 88%lowered it: lowest vs highest starters

1,313 participants with a Pre and a Post answer, Point-1 workshop. Medians, because a few typed answers were extreme.

2. The short answer

The best predictor is the person's own starting figure: the higher they began, the more likely they were to lower it.

Nothing else measured before the workshop adds to that, except that later batches lowered slightly less often. Much of the pattern is the natural pull of very high first answers back towards the middle, so read it as a description, not as proof the workshop caused it.

Think of it like guessing a house price. Ask a room of young people, "what does a good family house cost?" Ask again after two days of real talk. Most guesses come down and bunch together. The wildest guesses fall furthest, partly because they had the most room to fall.

4. Was it a meaningful discovery?

Step 1 found the pattern and Step 2 re-tested the same question with five independent methods. Reading both, the findings fall into three groups.

Meaningful

A large, broad shift towards more modest income expectations

Six in ten lowered their figure and only about one in seven raised it. After the workshop, answers are also much more tightly bunched (the spread shrinks by about 40%). Neither of these is explained by the "room to fall" effect, so this is the solid finding. It is an association only, since there is no comparison group.

Confirmed, but largely expected

"People who start high lower it most"

All five methods agree, so it is reliable. But it is close to built in: the drop is calculated from the starting number, and high one-off answers tend to come back down on a second ask. Step 2's fifth method found the pattern sits inside what pure noise would produce, so it says little about who the workshop moves. It is a useful fact, not an insight about people.

Not found or still open

No personal trait predicts it, and the mentor lead was never tested

Life priorities, career plans, life satisfaction, gender and age add nothing. That is a useful negative result: the shift is not confined to one kind of participant. Step 1's one lead, that having a life mentor makes lowering less likely, came from only 414 answers, was never verified, and was not included in Step 2's checks. The later-batch effect is new and unexplained.

In short: a meaningful description of change, a confirmed but mostly mechanical predictor, and no new driver. Step 1 rated itself 45% confident. Step 2 reached 4 of 5 methods in agreement.

NIRMAN programme directors: what this means

NIRMAN is run by SEARCH with MKCL to find and support young people who want to work on social problems. Participants go through an application, an interview, a first five-day workshop with mentoring, an action project and further workshops. The survey in this report sits at the first workshop (Point 1): the same question asked on arrival and on leaving.

What the data says to you

  • Expectations come down, broadly. Six in ten lowered their figure, and answers bunch closer together afterwards. It is not confined to one type of participant.
  • The starting figure is not a targeting tool. It predicts the drop mostly because of how numbers behave when asked twice. It does not tell you who the workshop moved.
  • No profile stands out. Career plans, life priorities, satisfaction, gender and age did not separate those who lowered it from those who did not.

These describe patterns, not the effect of the workshop, because there is no comparison group. Programme background is from the NIRMAN website.

5. How we arrived at the answer

Two rounds this time. Step 1 discovered an answer; Step 2 took that answer and re-checked it on the same question with five different methods.

Human question

What predicts a reduction in the income expected at age 30?
▼

Step 1: multi-step discovery

Five planned analyses on the Point-1 Pre/Post pairs. Two returned results, three came back empty.
▼

Answer (45% confidence)

63% lowered their figure. A high starting figure is the one clear predictor. A life mentor is an unconfirmed lead.
▼ handed on as the claim to test

Step 2: validation (5 methods)

Does a higher starting figure predict a larger drop? Tested five ways, including one that removes the "room to fall" effect.
▼

Validated answer (4 of 5 agree)

Starting figure is the main predictor (88% vs 33%). Later batch is the only other signal. Largely regression to the mean, an association only.

Technical detail

7. How Step 2 checked the claim: five methods

RunMethodWhat it foundVerdict
1Pearson correlation and linear regression, raw and log incomer = 0.87 raw, 0.64 log. Post-on-Pre slope 0.27, well below 1.Aligned
2Spearman rank correlation, Mann-Whitney U, quartile mediansρ = 0.69. Reducers started at ₹1.2 lakh vs ₹60k. Lowering rate 33% → 63% → 77% → 88%.Aligned
3Logistic regression with pre-workshop controls, test AUCOR 2.71 per SD of log starting figure, AUC 0.74. Other predictors add −0.001. Later batch OR 0.68.Aligned
4Outlier sensitivity: drop out-of-range, 5% trim, clipDirection holds in all three (N 1,125 to 1,313). Strength varies: Pearson 0.75 to 0.87.Aligned
5Regression-to-the-mean correction: % change, Oldham's method, noise simulationSpread of answers shrinks (variance ratio 0.61). Observed correlation falls inside the pure-noise range.Partly supported

The disagreement in Run 5 is about how strictly to label the result, not about the numbers, which match across runs. All runs use the same 1,313 pairs, so they show consistency, not independent proof.

8. Step 1's decision path (human in the loop)

At each step four next moves were proposed and one was chosen. Only two of the five steps returned numbers, which is why Step 1 rated itself 45% confident.

Results returned1. Build the targetChoice: screen factors, adjusting for starting income
No output2. Screen factors one at a timeChoice: re-run with diagnostics, then model
Results returned3. Re-screen, gated joint modelChoice: fix missing data, build baseline first
No output4. Does anything add to starting income?Choice: re-run in small stages
No output5. Baseline vs augmented model, mentor includedChoice: one stage per step

Step 3's joint model ran out of rows because items like the mentor question were asked in only some batches (414 answers). That is why the mentor lead stayed unverified.

11. Things to keep in mind

  • No comparison group. Everyone attended, so we cannot say the workshop caused the drop. Realism, regression to the mean or survey fatigue could all contribute.
  • A third of participants are missing. About 700 people answered Pre but not Post. Step 1 suggested checking whether they differ; this was not done.
  • "Lowered" includes tiny changes, down to ₹1,000, which may just be rounding.
  • Small count differences. Step 1 counts 828 or 827 people who lowered their figure, depending on capping; Step 2 uses 827.
  • The mentor lead and the batch effect are open questions for a follow-up.
  • Money-attitude items were not tested in Step 2, for example "knows the difference between threshold and aspirational income" or "values work freedom over financial gain". These are the most natural candidates for explaining why expectations fall.
